paragraphs.heading: Staying or leaving
paragraphs.text: Escape velocity is used to work out whether an object will stay inside a body's gravitational reach or leave it. The more speed an object has, the more places it can reach, and with enough energy every distance out to infinity is open to it. In energy terms, an object has reached escape velocity once its specific orbital energy, which is essentially its kinetic plus potential energy divided by its mass, is zero or more. Strictly it is a speed rather than a velocity, since direction does not matter.

paragraphs.heading: What it depends on
paragraphs.text: Escape speed depends on mass, because the pull of gravity between two objects depends on their combined mass. For a satellite or other small object, its own mass adds almost nothing and is usually ignored. Escape speed also changes with distance from the centre of the body. An object in a circular or elliptical orbit always moves slower than the escape speed where it is, while one on a hyperbolic path always moves faster. On the borderline parabolic path it moves at exactly escape speed, slowing forever toward zero but never quite stopping.

paragraphs.heading: Leaving Earth
paragraphs.text: From Earth, the escape velocity is 11.186 km/s, or about 40,270 km/h. A handy formula at a body's surface is vₑ = √2gr, where r is the distance from the body's centre and g is the pull of gravity there. In most cases it is not practical to reach that speed almost at once: the acceleration involved is too great, and in Earth's atmosphere such speeds would make most objects burn up or be torn apart. Instead, a spacecraft speeds up steadily as it climbs out of the air, until it reaches the escape velocity for its height, which is lower than at the surface.

paragraphs.heading: A head start from orbit
paragraphs.text: Often a spacecraft is first placed in a parking orbit, such as a low Earth orbit, and then sped up from there. At 200 km up, escape velocity is about 11.0 km/s, but the craft is already moving at roughly 7.8 km/s in orbit, so the extra speed it needs is much smaller. In general, escape velocity at any height is √2 times the speed of a circular orbit at that height. The circular-orbit speed is sometimes called the first cosmic velocity, and escape velocity the second cosmic velocity.

paragraphs.heading: The spinning Earth helps
paragraphs.text: These figures are measured in a frame that does not rotate. Earth's surface does rotate, so the speed a rocket needs relative to the ground depends on the direction it heads. At the equator the ground moves at 465 m/s, so a rocket launched east needs about 10.735 km/s relative to the surface, while one launched west needs about 11.665 km/s. The ground speed shrinks toward the poles, so launch sites such as Cape Canaveral and the Guiana Space Centre are placed as close to the equator as is practical.

paragraphs.heading: Other ways out
paragraphs.text: A rocket does not have to reach escape velocity in one burn. Under steady or repeated thrust it can in principle escape while moving at any speed above zero, although the least energy needed stays the same. Spacecraft can also take kinetic energy from large bodies through a gravity assist. And on an elliptical orbit, the change in speed needed to escape is smallest at the point closest to the central body, an effect explained by the Oberth effect.
